raw_evidence.label: Revenue grew 61x: $3.5B to $216B (FY2011-FY2026)
raw_evidence.content: NVIDIA's annual revenue rose from $3.54B in the fiscal year ending January 2011 to $215.94B in the fiscal year ending January 2026 — a 60.9x increase. Growth was modest and even negative through the gaming era (FY-end 2014 fell 3.5%, FY-end 2020 fell 6.8%), accelerated to 50-60% in FY-end 2021 and 2022, then went vertical: +125.9% (FY-end 2024), +114.2% (FY-end 2025), and +65.5% (FY-end 2026). The curve is not a smooth exponential — it is a flat decade followed by a near-vertical cliff starting in the fiscal year ending January 2024.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_01: Revenue trajectory FY2011-FY2026 ---
print("=== ana_01 ===")
ann["revenue_b"] = ann["revenue"].apply(b)
ann["rev_yoy_pct"] = (ann["revenue"].pct_change() * 100).round(1)
print(ann[["fy_end_year", "period_end", "revenue_b", "rev_yoy_pct"]].to_string(index=False))
print(f"FY2011 revenue: ${b(ann.iloc[0]['revenue'])}B -> FY2026 revenue: ${b(ann.iloc[-1]['revenue'])}B")
print(f"Total multiple FY2011->FY2026: {round(ann.iloc[-1]['revenue']/ann.iloc[0]['revenue'],1)}x")

raw_evidence.label: Net income grew 474x: $0.25B to $120B
raw_evidence.content: Net income — the split-immune profit measure — grew from $0.25B in FY-end 2011 to $120.07B in FY-end 2026, a 474x increase. The acceleration mirrors revenue but is even steeper because margins expanded at the same time: profit jumped from $4.37B (FY-end 2023) to $29.76B (FY-end 2024), then to $72.88B (FY-end 2025, +144.9%) and $120.07B (FY-end 2026). NVIDIA went from earning a quarter of a billion dollars a year to earning more than $120 billion.

ni2025 = ann[ann["fy_end_year"]==2025]["net_income"].iloc[0]
ni2026 = ann[ann["fy_end_year"]==2026]["net_income"].iloc[0]

print(f"Net income FY2011 ${b(ann.iloc[0]['net_income'])}B -> FY2026 ${b(ni2026)}B = {round(ni2026/ann.iloc[0]['net_income'],0)}x")

raw_evidence.label: From Denny's to the GPU: NVIDIA's origin
raw_evidence.content: NVIDIA was founded in 1993 by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem, reportedly over a meeting at a Denny's in East San Jose, with the goal of bringing advanced 3D graphics to gaming and multimedia. Its defining early moment was the 1999 GeForce 256, marketed as the world's first GPU. For most of its history NVIDIA was a graphics-and-gaming company — context that makes the later AI-driven revenue explosion in this dataset all the more dramatic. The earliest years in this dataset (FY2011-FY2016, revenue in the $3.5B-$5B range) represent that gaming-centric era, before data center became the dominant business.

raw_evidence.label: The FY2024 inflection: data center +427%
raw_evidence.content: Fiscal 2024 (covering most of calendar 2023) was the hinge of the entire AI story. NVIDIA reported full-year revenue of about $26.0B for FY2023 that was essentially flat, then in FY2024 total revenue rocketed up 262% year-over-year to roughly $60.9B, with Data Center revenue alone up 427% as hyperscalers raced to buy Hopper-architecture H100 GPUs to train large language models. Q4 FY2024 data center compute revenue was up 478% year-over-year. This single inflection — from a flat year to a tripling — is the most important external fact for interpreting the revenue trend in this dataset.

raw_evidence.label: FY2023: the flat year before the boom
raw_evidence.content: It is easy to forget that immediately before the explosion, NVIDIA had a rough year. Fiscal 2023 revenue was roughly $26.97B, essentially flat versus the prior year, as the gaming segment fell about 27% to $9.07B amid a post-crypto-mining glut, channel-inventory corrections, and weak macro conditions. Net margin in this dataset collapses from 36.2% in FY2022 to 16.2% in FY2023 — the worst margin in the AI-era window — before snapping back to 48.9% in FY2024. This makes FY2023 the dramatic 'before' that sets up the 'after', and explains the V-shaped dip visible in any margin chart.

Source: NVDA Stock Split History (https://www.bitget.com/wiki/nvda-stock-split-history) Facts: NVIDIA executed a 4-for-1 split in July 2021 and a 10-for-1 split in June 2024; The 10-for-1 split followed the share price surpassing $1,000

raw_evidence.label: EPS is not split-adjusted; prices are
raw_evidence.content: A central caveat that shapes how this data must be read: SEC reports earnings-per-share exactly as filed, so EPS is NOT adjusted for stock splits, while the stock prices ARE split-adjusted. The visible symptom is that diluted EPS appears to collapse across a split even when profits soared — FY2024 diluted EPS of $11.93 'drops' to $2.94 in FY2025 across the 10:1 split, despite net income more than doubling. The clean, split-immune way to track the business is net income, which rose from $29.8B to $72.9B over exactly that span. Plotting raw EPS against split-adjusted price on one axis would be misleading; net income against price is the honest comparison.

raw_evidence.label: The EPS trap: looks like a 75% drop, was a doubling
raw_evidence.content: This is the most important interpretive caveat in the dataset. Reported diluted EPS appears to fall from $11.93 (FY-end 2024) to $2.94 (FY-end 2025) — a 75% 'collapse' — yet net income over the same period rose from $29.76B to $72.88B. The reason: NVIDIA executed a 10-for-1 stock split in June 2024, and SEC EPS is reported as-filed (not split-adjusted), so the share count multiplied by ten. On a like-for-like basis, $11.93 becomes $1.19 post-split, which means the actual $2.94 reported is more than double. Anyone plotting raw EPS against the split-adjusted price would see a fake crash; net income is the honest series.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_05: The EPS split trap ---
print("=== ana_05 ===")
eps = ann[ann["fy_end_year"].isin([2024,2025,2026])][["fy_end_year","eps_diluted","net_income"]].copy()
eps["net_income_b"] = eps["net_income"].apply(b)
print(eps[["fy_end_year","eps_diluted","net_income_b"]].to_string(index=False))
print("EPS 'falls' 11.93 -> 2.94 across the 10:1 split while net income MORE THAN DOUBLES.")
print("11.93 / 10 = 1.193 (post-split-equivalent); reported 2.94 is HIGHER because earnings grew.")

raw_evidence.label: Two splits and the $5 trillion market cap
raw_evidence.content: The market's verdict on this revenue story was historic. NVIDIA's share price rose so far that it executed a 4-for-1 split in July 2021 and a 10-for-1 split in June 2024 (when shares had passed $1,000). On October 29, 2025 NVIDIA became the first public company ever to reach a $5 trillion market capitalization, and by spring 2026 it was the world's most valuable company at roughly $5.2 trillion, with split-adjusted shares around $216. The split-adjusted price series in this dataset — rising from cents in the 2010s to over $200 by FY2026 — is the market pricing in the revenue curve.

The stock prices come from Yahoo Finance via yfinance with auto_adjust enabled, so they are fully adjusted for NVIDIA's two stock splits (4:1 in 2021, 10:1 in 2024) and dividends. The annual file covers fiscal years 2011 through 2026. A crucial structural detail: NVIDIA's fiscal year ends in late January, so 'FY2026' mostly covers calendar 2025 — the period_end column carries the authoritative date, and any join between financials and prices must use period_end, not the year label.

raw_evidence.label: CUDA and AlexNet: the accelerated-computing pivot
raw_evidence.content: NVIDIA's transformation from graphics vendor to AI infrastructure company traces to two events. In 2006 it introduced CUDA, a parallel-computing platform that let developers run general-purpose computation on GPUs. In 2012, GPUs powered the breakthrough AlexNet neural network, kicking off the deep-learning era and making NVIDIA's hardware the default substrate for AI. The company now states that over 90% of all AI training in the world happens on NVIDIA GPUs. This is the why behind the numbers: the revenue curve in this dataset is the financial shadow of NVIDIA becoming the picks-and-shovels supplier of the AI gold rush.

raw_evidence.label: FY2023: the flat year before the boom
raw_evidence.content: It is easy to forget that immediately before the explosion, NVIDIA had a rough year. Fiscal 2023 revenue was roughly $26.97B, essentially flat versus the prior year, as the gaming segment fell about 27% to $9.07B amid a post-crypto-mining glut, channel-inventory corrections, and weak macro conditions. Net margin in this dataset collapses from 36.2% in FY2022 to 16.2% in FY2023 — the worst margin in the AI-era window — before snapping back to 48.9% in FY2024. This makes FY2023 the dramatic 'before' that sets up the 'after', and explains the V-shaped dip visible in any margin chart.
